newsitem.title: USA: Divided ethics panel meets on Gingrich probe.
newsitem.headline: Divided ethics panel meets on Gingrich probe.

text.p: A sharply divided House of Representatives Ethics Committee met on Wednesday to clear the way for the final phase of its investigation of Speaker Newt Gingrich one day after the House refused to give it more time.
Under rules adopted on Tuesday, the House must vote on penalties for Gingrich's admitted ethics violations by Jan. 21.
After five hours of meeting behind closed doors, Committee Chairwomen Nancy Johnson, R-Connecticut, said the committee was working on a schedule and promised more information later in the day.
She told reporters: "We're working together, and we're doing well."
The Jan. 21 date was agreed on by the committee last month but investigators said on Tuesday they needed more time to ensure a "fair and orderly" process.

Democrats sought on Tuesday to eliminate a provision in the House rules that would put the current ethics committee out of business after Jan. 21, but they were blocked by the House in a virtual party line vote that split the ethics panel. The two Republicans on a four-member subcommittee that has been investigating Gingrich backed the call for more time.
The vote came less than three hours after Gingrich was re-elected speaker, with nine Republicans deserting him because of his ethics problems.

He admitted on Dec. 21 he had failed to get legal advice to ensure compliance with a ban on using tax-exempt funds for partisan political activity and had given false information to investigators, which he has said was unintentional.
The call for extra time for the last phase of the investigation was spelled out in a statement on Tuesday by James Cole, a special counsel leading the probe.

"In analysing the time necessary for a sanctions hearing and a vote on the House floor, I have recommended a schedule that will allow this to be accomplished in a fair and orderly fashion," he said. "In doing that, however, it will be necessary for the vote on the House floor to occur after Jan. 21, 1977."

Cole said the subcommittee agreed with this view. But full ethics committee member David Hobson, an Ohio Republican, told the House the Democratic motion, which contained no end-date, meant the affair could "go on forever and ever."

Representative Jim McDermott of Washington, the top Democrat on the full committee, said Gingrich's attorney had called Cole on Monday to say he would not be ready for hearings until Jan. 13 and needed time to prepare.

"We are being forced into a schedule which is being designed for political damage control," McDermott said, charging that Republicans wanted to have the House vote on Jan. 20 -- presidential inauguration day.
